parole.significato: cave (space or cavity formed underground, especially between rocks, or in the face of a cliff or hillside)
parole.testo: The usual theory considers ala to be borrowed from Middle Low German hol (“depth, hole, cave”), from Old Saxon hol, or maybe from the same form in Middle Dutch or German Low German (East Frisian); cf. German Höhle (“cave”), all from Proto-West Germanic *hol. A different view suggests that ala could

parole.significato: common bleak (small river fish of the family Cyprinidae, species Alburnus alburnus)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German alat, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *al- (“white, shiny”), first mentioned in 18th-century sources.

parole.significato: picture, image
parole.testo: From Middle Low German bilde or Middle Dutch bilde (“drawing, image, example”), cf. German Bild.

parole.significato: ink
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German blak, black, from Old Saxon *blak, from Proto-West Germanic *blak, from Proto-Germanic *blakaz, still mentioned in late 19th-century dictionaries, but since then replaced by another 19th-century borrowing, tinte.

parole.significato: breakfast (the morning meal; also, the time or occasion of that meal)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German vrōkost (cf. Swedish frukost “breakfast,” and also the German older term Frühkost “breakfast,” literally “early food”). The initial cluster was changed from vr [fr] to br to conform to Latvian patterns; the final ost changed to ast perhaps under the influence of words

parole.significato: brown (having the color of, e.g., chocolate, or of the ground coffee)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German brūn and (perhaps) Middle Dutch bruun. This term was probably introduced in the 15th century, together with brown-colored clothes, very appreciated at the time. It is, however, not mentioned in dictionaries until the end of the 17th and the beginning of the 18th centu

parole.significato: ditch
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German grav.

parole.significato: cucumber (plant of the family Cucurbitaceae, species Cucumis sativus, often cultivated in gardens for its edible vegeta…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German augurke (cf. German Gurke); the Germanic term is itself a borrowing from Polish ogórek, originally from Greek άγουρος (ágouros) “unripe, immature”) which replaced an earlier term krievāboli. First attested in 17th-century dictionaries as augurķis, later agurķe, agurķi

parole.significato: office (room)
parole.testo: Akin to Middle Low German kantôr, German Kontor, Russian контора (kontora), Lithuanian kontora. Regardless of the intermediate (or presence/absence thereof), ultimately from Middle Low German kontôr, komtôr, komptor (“commercial branch; writing room; counting desk/table”), from Middle Dutch contoor,

parole.significato: rock, cliff (massif with steep edges; rocky cliff)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German klint (“rocky coast, slope, cliff”). The word entered Latvian in the 18th century from Baltic German dialects; prior to that, akmens “stone,” often in combination with other terms, was used instead.

parole.significato: dead body, corpse (the body of a dead person)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German lik (cf. Old Saxon līk, German Leiche), more specifically from the version of Baltic (Low) German spoken in Latvia in the 18th century, when the first recorded attestations occur. Previously, only its synonym mironis was used to express this meaning.

parole.significato: color, paint
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German verwe (“color, paint”), from Old Saxon farwi, from Proto-West Germanic *faru; compare German Farbe, Dutch verf.

parole.significato: pitch
parole.testo: From Middle Low German pik or Middle Dutch pick (cf. German Pech) which, in turn, from Latin pix. From the latter (via Russian) also Latvian pekle (“hell”).

parole.significato: priest (male religious official trained to perform and lead rituals at a church or temple)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German prēster, or maybe from Middle Dutch preester (cf. German Priester), itself a borrowing from Late Latin presbyter, borrowed from Ancient Greek πρεσβύτερος (presbúteros), from πρέσβυς (présbus, “elder, older”). The Latvian term is first mentioned in 17th-century sources

parole.significato: bottle (container with a tapered top for storing liquids)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German buddel, itself borrowed from French bouteille, from Late Latin buticula, the diminutive form of buttis (“barrel”), from Ancient Greek βοῦθις (boûthis, “barrel”). The word is first mentioned as budele in 18th-century dictionaries; the current form (with b > p, perhaps

parole.significato: clock, watch (instrument to measure time)
parole.testo: There are various theories about the origin of this word, originally meaning “church bell.” The most likely to be true derives it from an unattested verb *pulsēt (“to produce sound”) (compare archaic pulstens, dialectal pulstenis (“bell”), pulkstiens (“bell sound, toll”)) > *pulksēt with an epenthet

parole.significato: Pope (the bishop of Rome, the head of the Catholic Church and ruler of the Vatican City State)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German pāwest (“Pope”) (compare German Papst), from an earlier pāwes (with an intrusive final t), borrowed from Old French papes, also borrowed from Medieval Latin pāpa (in use for the bishop of Rome since the 5th century), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek πάππας (páppas,

parole.significato: color, paint
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German verwe (“color, paint”), from Old Saxon farwi, from Proto-West Germanic *faru; compare German Farbe, Dutch verf.

parole.significato: wardrobe; cupboard; closet; shelf
parole.testo: From Middle Low German schap, from Old Saxon skap, from Proto-West Germanic *skap (“shape”), from Proto-Germanic *skapą.

parole.significato: bucket, pail (cylindrical metal, wooden, or plastic container with a handle)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German span (“wooden bucket”), likely from the same ultimate source as English span, similar to Swedish spann (“pail, bucket”). This generated the dialectal form spanis, spannis; in Kurzeme, also *spandis > spaņģis (with ģ probably from genitive *spandya); compare Lithuanian

parole.significato: bacon, lard (subcutaneous fat layer on a pig; slice of pork containing such fat)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German speck, or from Middle Dutch speck (cf. German Speck, Dutch spek), first mentioned in 17th-century dictionaries.

parole.significato: play
parole.testo: Likely from Middle Low German spel, from Old Saxon spil, from Proto-West Germanic *spil. Cognate with German Spiel.

parole.significato: old unit for measuring volume, equivalent to approximately 1.3 cubic decimeters
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German stōp (“measure of volume”), first mentioned in 17th-century dictionaries.

parole.significato: hour (a time period of 60 minutes)
parole.testo: A borrowing, traditionally described as from Middle Low German stunde (“hour”), from Old Saxon stunda, from Proto-West Germanic *stundu, from Proto-Germanic *stundō, since this form is found in the earliest attestations. But some authors argue that these early attestations are found only in some dia

parole.significato: tent
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German telt (“tent”). Compare German Zelt. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *del- (“split, cut”), whence Proto-Germanic *teldą. From the same Proto-Indo-European source Latvian dalīt (“divide”), deldēt (“wear out”).

parole.significato: tower (tall, cylindrical or similarly shaped structure in a building)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German torn or Middle Dutch toorn or an East Frisian word (compare West Frisian toer; also compare German Turm), itself a borrowing, via Old Frisian torn, from Latin turris (accusative turrem). A dialectal German form Turn, borrowed as turnis, would in the Kurzeme dialects y

parole.significato: ladders
parole.testo: From Middle Low German treppe, trappe. Compare German Treppe.

parole.significato: additive conjunction used to link similar terms in a clause; and
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German un (“and”). It replaced, in this sense, the particle ir (compare Lithuanian ir, which still has the sense of “and”). Variants were und, unde and ind, in and may have been influenced by ir, but ind also existed in Middle Low German. From the 18th century onward, the fo

parole.significato: bathtub, tub (large container for water in which a person may bathe or wash something)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German wanne or Swedish vanna (cf. German Wanne), itself a borrowing from Latin vannus (“winnowing basket”). Such baskets were originally long and round; bathtubs were named after them due to the resemblance in form. The term is first mentioned in Latvian in 17th- and 18th-c

parole.significato: boy (male child, especially of school age; also, male adolescent)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German sönke (“son (dim.”) (also sänke), borrowed in parallel to zēns from the non-diminutive form söhn, sȫne.

parole.significato: soap (substance, synthetic or derived from fats, used for washing, usually in the form of a bar or as a liquid)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German sepe, seepe or Middle Dutch zepe “soap,” first attested in Latvian in 17th-century dictionaries.

parole.significato: saw (a tool with a sharp, usually toothed, blade, used for cutting wood, metal and other hard substances)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German sage or Middle Dutch zage (cf. German Säge, Dutch zaag). First mentioned in 17th-century dictionaries.

parole.significato: boy (a male child, approximately until 11 years of age)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German söhn (“son”) (sȫne); cf. Sohn (“son”). The e is the nearest vowel to ö in Latvian; the length probably results from the influence of dēls (“son”). In an 18th-century dictionary, zēns is mentioned as “rarely used,” and only in the area around Riga and in Courland; in t

parole.significato: ide (small fish species of the family Cyprinidae, species Leuciscus idus)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German ālant, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *al- (“white, shiny”), first mentioned in 17th-century sources (as alands; the form ālants appeared only in the 19th century).

parole.significato: ice hole
parole.testo: From Middle Low German (dialectal) hāling. Cognate with Lithuanian ólingis, ólingė, Latgalian uoliņgis.

parole.significato: hook (instrument with a curved extremity ending in a pointed tip, used to hang or suspend things)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German hake or Middle Dutch haeck or an East Frisian word (compare Saterland Frisian Hoake (“hook”), German Haken), all ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *keg-, *kek- (“peg, hook; to bend”).

parole.significato: yew
parole.testo: From Middle Low German īve, ībe (“yew”), from Proto-Germanic *īwō (“yew”). Via Proto-Indo-European, a doublet of iẽva (“hagberry”).

parole.significato: to comb (to smooth with a comb)
parole.testo: From ķemme (“comb”), a borrowing from Low German, made into a second conjugation verb stem (ending -ēt). Alternatively, it may be a direct borrowing from Middle Low German [Term?] (cf. German kämmen (“to comb”)). First mentioned in 17th-century sources.

parole.significato: garlic (herbaceous plant, sp. Allium sativum, with pungent edible bulbs)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German klüflōk (“garlic”) (cf. German Knoblauch, Dutch knoflook), with klüf- from Proto-Germanic *kliuban (“to split, to cut”) and -lōk “onion, leek” (cf. German Lauch, Dutch look, English leek), i.e., originally “split, segmented onion.” This loanword is first mentioned in

parole.significato: cherry tree
parole.testo: From Middle Low German kerse, from Proto-West Germanic *kirsijā. Compare German Kirsche, Estonian kirss, Finnish kirsikka.

parole.significato: ham
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German schinke, schink. Compare German Schinken.

parole.significato: scissors (tool for cutting, consisting of two interconnected blades facing each other)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German schere or from Middle Dutch scheer, both meaning “scissors” (cf. also German Schere). It is first mentioned in 17th-century dictionaries.

parole.significato: pants, trousers; shorts (outer garment that covers the lower body from the waist down, with two long or short legs)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German büxe, bükse, or from Old Frisian büxe, bükse; cf. German dialectal buxe, Swedish byxa, byxor, first mentioned in 17th-century dictionaries. The original meaning was “goat leather pants” (cf. Middle Low German buck “male goat,” “buck”), later extended to all kinds of p

parole.significato: arrow (long, thin projectile to be shot with a bow or crossbow)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German bolte (“bolt”), or from Middle Dutch bult (“bolt”) (compare German Bolzen, English bolt), first mentioned in 17th-century dictionaries.

parole.significato: ship (fairly large vehicle on water)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German kogge (“wide, roundish ship”), or from Old Frisian kogge, Middle Dutch kogge, or perhaps from Old Norse kuggi (“sea vessel”) or Swedish kogg (“merchant ship”). The word was first used in Germanic languages to refer to a kind of sail, wide with stumpy, roundish ends; i

parole.significato: daughter (a female child, with respect to her parents)
parole.testo: Traditionally, this word is considered borrowed from Middle Low German meid (“female servant”) (or from Middle High German meyt, meyde, or Middle Dutch meit), which replaced an older Proto-Indo-European word, probably *dukte, cognate with Lithuanian duktė̃, Old Prussian duckti, Russian дочь (doč’),

parole.significato: rose (decorative shrub, gen. Rosa, with beautiful flowers and thorny stems)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German rōse, or from Middle Dutch rōse (compare German Rose), themselves borrowings from Latin rosa. The word was also apparently borrowed into Latin (via Ancient Greek) from Old Persian. In Latvian texts this word is first mentioned in the 16th century, apparently as a gene

parole.significato: bad ((of people) not following moral rules, treating others in a cruel or insensitive way; (of their actions) typical o…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German slicht (“plain, simple, common, without value, inferior, inappropriate”), or from Middle Dutch slicht (“simple, common”); compare German schlecht (“bad, evil”). First found in 17th- and 18th-century dictionaries, still marked as a Germanism; at that time, the word men

parole.significato: sick, ill, diseased (having a disturbance in the normal functioning of the body or one or some of its parts)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German slim or from Middle Dutch slim (“twisted, crooked; bad, evil”); compare also German schlimm (“bad, evil; (col.) sick”). First attested in the 17th century, mostly with meanings such as “bad”, “useless”, “inappropriate”, “evil”, or “wild”, or more rarely “sick”. This l

parole.significato: mirror; synonym of spogulis
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German spegel, or from Middle Dutch spegel (compare German Spiegel, Dutch spiegel), now mostly replaced by spogulis (q.v.).

parole.significato: wine (alcoholic drink made from berriess or fruit juices)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German wīn, or from Old Norse vín or Middle Dutch wijn, wiin (cf. German Wein, Swedish vin, Dutch wijn, English wine), or maybe also from Old East Slavic вино (vino), Russian вино́ (vinó), itself a borrowing from Latin vīnum, which is a possible borrowing from an old Mediter

parole.significato: chain (sequence of interconnected, usually metal, rings or links)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German kede, or from Middle Dutch cede (cf. German Kette), themselves borrowings from Latin catena, ultimately from a Proto-Indo-European stem *kat- (“to weave, to braid”). This is an old borrowing, already mentioned in 17th-century sources, sometimes with a prothetic š (šķē

parole.significato: king (the monarch of a kingdom)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German könink (“king”), or from Middle Dutch coninc (“ruler”) (cf. German König, Dutch koning, English king), parallel forms to Middle Low German kunig (whence Latvian kùngs (“lord, sir, Mr.”), q.v.).
